title: Parallel Channels Out of the Eye

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: The retina's only output neurons are {{c1::ganglion cells}}, whose axons form the optic nerve.
cards.quote: Every signal the brain receives from the eye leaves through ganglion cells, the retina's only output neurons, whose axons make the optic nerve.

cards.front: Why does the optic nerve carry multiple filtered views of a scene?
cards.back: Bipolar and amacrine circuits build different filters before ganglion cells send spikes; distinct ganglion cell types report different features of the same scene.
cards.quote: Bipolar and amacrine circuits inside the retina build each filter before any spike leaves the eye,

cards.front: Two scenes produce identical signals in every retinal output channel but differ in a feature none carries. Can combining channels in the brain recover that difference, and why?
cards.back: No. The rule is that information absent from every retinal channel is lost before reaching the brain. Combining channels can build new features only from the information delivered.
cards.quote: Information that no channel carries is gone before the brain has a chance, though the brain can combine channels into new features.

cards.front: What motion pattern strongly activates a W3 ganglion cell in isolated mouse retina, and what pattern largely silences it?
cards.back: A small object moving over a still background activates it; whole-scene motion largely silences it.
cards.quote: So a W3 cell answers one question: is something small moving differently from everything else?
cards.section: One cell that ignores the world moving

cards.front: Why do ON and OFF inputs to a mouse W3 cell add rather than cancel?
cards.back: Each input is rectified: it excites for its own sign of brightness change and contributes little for the other. Both brightening and dimming can therefore excite W3.
cards.quote: Each input is "rectified": it drives the cell for its own sign of change and does little for the other.
cards.section: One cell that ignores the world moving

cards.front: How does distant-surround motion suppress a mouse W3 cell at both presynaptic and postsynaptic sites?
cards.back: Presynaptically, less excitation reaches W3. Postsynaptically, inhibition acts on W3 itself. The presynaptic input terminals responsible are not specified.
cards.quote: Part is postsynaptic: inhibition lands on the W3 cell itself.
cards.section: One cell that ignores the world moving

cards.front: Which amacrine cell supplies much of the excitation to mouse W3 cells, and which amacrine class is the proposed global-motion brake?
cards.back: VG3 amacrine cells supply excitation; wide-field amacrine cells are the proposed brake.
cards.quote: Keep the two amacrine cells apart: the VG3 cell brings excitation in, and wide-field amacrine cells are the proposed brake.
cards.section: One cell that ignores the world moving

cards.front: In an isolated retina, a ganglion cell fires less when a distant surround moves. Its centre receives identical motion in both trials. What does this control show?
cards.back: The distant surround suppresses the response; a change in the centre stimulus cannot explain the reduction. This comparison alone does not locate the suppression within the circuit.
cards.quote: It does not, so motion far outside the centre must be silencing it.
cards.section: One cell that ignores the world moving

cards.front: A retinal neuron responds selectively to a small moving object in isolated tissue. Design a test of whether its activity is necessary for an animal to respond to that object.
cards.back: Selectively suppress the candidate cells and compare the behavioural response with a matched control. The rule is that isolated-tissue selectivity establishes a filter, not behavioural necessity; necessity requires testing behaviour during perturbation.
cards.quote: the experiments established selectivity and circuit properties ex vivo, and no behavioural test of necessity was done.
cards.section: One cell that ignores the world moving

cards.front: Why does a mouse W3 cell falling silent during whole-scene motion not imply that the brain receives no scene-motion information?
cards.back: Other retinal channels still carry scene motion. W3 silence reflects its own filter, rather than the information carried by every ganglion cell type.
cards.quote: The scene motion that W3 ignores still travels in other channels.
cards.section: One cell that ignores the world moving

cards.front: In isolated mouse retina, what direction do asymmetric JAM-B-labelled ganglion cells prefer, relative to their own shape?
cards.back: Movement from the soma toward the dendrites.
cards.quote: in isolated retina these asymmetric cells preferred movement from soma toward dendrites.
cards.section: JAM-B: a lopsided cell with a preferred direction

cards.front: A retinal neuron prefers a stimulus moving downward across the retinal image. With the lens inverting the image, which visual-field direction should activate it, and why?
cards.back: Upward motion in the visual field, because lens inversion reverses the direction between visual field and retinal image.
cards.quote: Because the lens inverts the image, that direction on the retina corresponds to upward motion in the visual field,
cards.section: JAM-B: a lopsided cell with a preferred direction

cards.front: What does “one type, one mosaic, one map” mean as a working picture of mouse retinal output?
cards.back: Cells of a type share broadly the same filter and usually form a spaced mosaic; together they sample the scene as one of many overlapping maps.
cards.quote: The one idea to carry through this lesson: one type, one mosaic, one map.
cards.section: JAM-B: a lopsided cell with a preferred direction

cards.front: A researcher assumes that every JAM-B-labelled cell throughout mouse retina must be direction-selective. What observation challenges that prediction, and why?
cards.back: Symmetric labelled cells in ventral retina showed no clear preferred direction. The filter can vary with retinal location, so the label alone does not guarantee uniform responses.
cards.quote: Symmetric labelled cells in ventral retina showed no clear preferred direction, so a type's filter may itself change across the retina.
cards.section: JAM-B: a lopsided cell with a preferred direction

cards.front: A retinal ganglion cell {{c1::functional}} type is a group of cells with the same light response.
cards.quote: A functional type is a group of cells with the same light response.
cards.section: Testing a type: agreement and a mosaic

cards.front: What is a transcriptomic cluster, and must it contain exactly one biological cell type?
cards.back: An algorithm-defined group of expression profiles; it may contain one type or several.
cards.quote: A cluster is different: it is the group an algorithm draws around such profiles, and it may hold one type or several.
cards.section: Testing a type: agreement and a mosaic

cards.front: How does an anatomical retinal ganglion cell type differ from a molecular type?
cards.back: An anatomical type shares dendritic shape and depth in the inner plexiform layer; a molecular type shares an expression profile.
cards.quote: A molecular type shares an expression profile.
cards.section: Testing a type: agreement and a mosaic

cards.front: What evidence strengthens the claim that a retinal cell cluster represents one real type?
cards.back: Agreement among response, shape and expression, plus a regular mosaic of cell bodies. Genetic access to label or manipulate the group strengthens the claim.
cards.quote: a transcriptomic or anatomical cluster becomes a type when response, shape and expression are tied to one another
cards.section: Testing a type: agreement and a mosaic

cards.front: A retinal cell group has regularly spaced cell bodies but strongly overlapping dendrites. Does the overlap contradict a mosaic, and why?
cards.back: No. A mosaic describes cell-body spacing; the dendrites of cells within one type can overlap extensively.
cards.quote: A mosaic describes the spacing of cell bodies; the dendrites of one type can still overlap a lot.
cards.section: Testing a type: agreement and a mosaic

cards.front: The average number of dendritic arbors covering a retinal location is the {{c1::coverage factor}}.
cards.back: Coverage factor = cell density (cells/mm²) × mean dendritic field area (mm²).
cards.quote: coverage factor = cell density (cells/mm²) × mean dendritic field area (mm²)
cards.section: Coverage: how a type samples the scene

cards.front: In a hypothetical uniform retinal region, one ganglion cell type has density 150 cells/mm² and mean dendritic field area 20,000 µm². Given 1 mm² = 1,000,000 µm², estimate its coverage factor.
cards.back: Area = 20,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 0.02 mm². Coverage = 150 cells/mm² × 0.02 mm² = 3: about 3 arbors cover an average point.
cards.quote: coverage factor = cell density (cells/mm²) × mean dendritic field area (mm²)
cards.section: Coverage: how a type samples the scene

cards.front: For mouse W3 cells, use peak density 440 cells/mm² and mean dendritic field area 10,300 µm² to estimate coverage. Use 1 µm² = 10⁻⁶ mm².
cards.back: Area = 10,300 × 10⁻⁶ = 0.0103 mm². Coverage = 440 × 0.0103 = 4.532, or 4.53: about 4.5 arbors per point. Pairing peak density with mean area makes this an estimate.
cards.quote: The figure also pairs a regional peak density with a mean area, so treat it as an estimate.
cards.section: Coverage: how a type samples the scene

cards.front: Why does merging two independently placed, regular retinal mosaics usually make cell-body spacing look less regular?
cards.back: Each type spaces its own cells apart, but cells of different types can sit close together. The merged group gains unusually short neighbour distances.
cards.quote: Each type keeps its own cells apart, but nothing stops a cell of one type from sitting right beside a cell of the other,
cards.section: Coverage: how a type samples the scene

cards.front: A retinal cluster has unusually close cell-body pairs and high coverage. How would you test a possible merge of types without treating either sign as proof?
cards.back: Look for response, shape or expression differences, then test spacing and coverage within the resulting groups. The rule is that merged mosaics can raise coverage and reduce regularity, but real types can also have these properties.
cards.quote: Neither sign proves a merge, since some real types are only weakly regular and some have high coverage,
cards.section: Coverage: how a type samples the scene

cards.front: If a TYW3-labelled mouse cell count included cells other than W3B, what would happen to coverage estimated for W3B using that density, and why?
cards.back: It would be overestimated, assuming the field area used is unchanged. The label marks several types, so the measured density could exceed the density of W3B alone.
cards.quote: if the density counted more than one of them, the density, and so the coverage, may be overestimated for W3B.
cards.section: Coverage: how a type samples the scene

cards.front: Why are imaging, RNA sequencing, same-cell recording and electron microscopy counts of mouse ganglion cell types not rival answers?
cards.back: They group cells by different evidence: light responses, expression, linked responses and molecular or shape data, or anatomy. Preparation and resolution differ; some counts are lower bounds.
cards.quote: Each reflects a method, a preparation and a resolution, and the most trustworthy types are the ones that more than one method finds.
cards.section: Four ways to count

cards.front: In the mouse electron-microscopy census, what do 47 and at least 35 count?
cards.back: 47 anatomical clusters; at least 35 validated or securely known types. The latter is a lower bound.
cards.quote: So 47 counts clusters, and 35 is a floor on types.
cards.section: Four ways to count

cards.front: Suppose the two known direction-selective types in one of Tran’s 45 mouse RNA clusters had been left merged. How would the reported type count compare with the refined atlas, and why?
cards.back: It would remain 45 rather than 46. Splitting the cluster adds one type, showing that clustering alone can miss distinctions established by function.
cards.quote: The authors split that cluster with a semi-supervised analysis, giving 46 types, so the count depends on prior knowledge as well as on the data.
cards.section: Four ways to count

cards.front: Three sustained ON direction-selective mouse groups share RNA cluster C10. What measurements would strengthen the case that they are distinct types?
cards.back: Record responses and recover RNA and shape from the same cells in each group, then test each group for its own mosaic. The rule is agreement across response, shape, expression and spacing; one shared RNA cluster need not mean one type.
cards.quote: Record the light response of many more cells in each class, then recover RNA and shape from those same cells.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Why does the primate foveal midget pathway preserve fine spatial detail?
cards.back: Each receptive-field centre receives a single cone’s signal through a private bipolar-to-ganglion pathway, preserving cone-array detail. The surround still pools neighbouring cones.
cards.quote: The fine spatial detail of the cone array. That is why midget cells support high-acuity vision.
cards.section: Mouse is not macaque: the primate fovea

cards.front: What response features characterize primate parasol ganglion cells?
cards.back: Transient responses and sensitivity to motion and low contrast.
cards.quote: Parasol cells respond transiently and are sensitive to motion and to low contrast, functionally like the transient alpha cells of rodents.
cards.section: Mouse is not macaque: the primate fovea

cards.front: In the sampled macaque foveal ganglion cells, midget clusters are about 85% and parasol clusters 11%. What fraction remains for other clusters, and how many cells would that represent in a hypothetical sample of 5,000?
cards.back: Midget plus parasol = 85% + 11% = 96%. Remainder = 100% − 96% = about 4%; 0.04 × 5,000 = about 200 cells. This does not give the number of other types.
cards.quote: The 4% says how much of the sample is left over, not how many types share it.
cards.section: Mouse is not macaque: the primate fovea

cards.front: A researcher assigns the macaque foveal midget percentage to the entire human retina. Is that inference supported, and why?
cards.back: No. The percentages describe sampled macaque foveal cells, not whole-retina or human frequencies. Species and retinal region matter.
cards.quote: The percentages are of sampled cells from the macaque fovea; they are not whole-retina figures and not human frequencies,
cards.section: Mouse is not macaque: the primate fovea

cards.front: Several retinal response classes share an expression cluster. Each class lacks its own regular mosaic, but all classes together form one. Which interpretation gains support, and what remains unresolved?
cards.back: One type with multiple response modes gains support. The rule is that a type usually has its own mosaic; however, spatial evidence alone cannot settle identity, so linked response, shape and expression evidence is still needed.
cards.quote: If the three classes together form one regular mosaic and none forms its own, that points toward one type with several response modes,
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A cell atlas reports a cell type’s percentage after sorting and dissociating tissue. A researcher calls it the type’s true tissue frequency. What limitation should change that interpretation?
cards.back: The percentage describes the processed sample. Sorting and dissociation can affect representation, so the sample share need not equal the frequency in intact tissue.
cards.quote: These are shares of flow-sorted, dissociated cells, which need not match the true frequencies of the types in the retina.
cards.section: The three functional and molecular censuses

cards.front: Tran’s mouse atlas contains 35,699 high-quality ganglion cell transcriptomes. Approximately how many represent a type at 0.15%, and why can its mosaic be difficult to assess in a small retinal patch?
cards.back: 0.15% = 0.15 ÷ 100 = 0.0015; 0.0015 × 35,699 = 53.5485, or about 54 sampled cells. A rare type may contribute few cells to a small patch, limiting a mosaic test.
cards.quote: A type this rare is also hard to test for a mosaic, since a small patch of retina may hold few of its cells.
cards.section: The three functional and molecular censuses

cards.front: Why does a reconstructed contact between two neurons not by itself prove a synaptic connection?
cards.back: Not every contact is a synapse. A contact map identifies candidate partners, but the contact alone does not establish synaptic connectivity.
cards.quote: The authors cautioned that not all contacts are synapses, so a contact map proposes partners and does not prove them.
cards.section: Dense reconstruction and the anatomical count

cards.front: What does the retinal density-conservation hypothesis propose should stay approximately uniform across the retina for a cell type?
cards.back: Aggregate dendritic density: total dendrite per unit retinal area, despite variation in cell density and arbor size. Coverage instead counts arbors.
cards.quote: the aggregate dendritic density of a type (its total dendrite per unit area of retina) should be about uniform across the retina,
cards.section: Density conservation

cards.front: In one mouse retinal patch, ganglion cells arborising at the inner IPL margin have more sustained responses on average. Does shape now identify functional type or establish causation? What evidence would strengthen the interpretation?
cards.back: Neither follows from the association alone. Link response, shape and expression in the same cells and test candidate mosaics. The rule is agreement across evidence for type identity; IPL depth helps set inputs but does not alone establish a causal explanation.
cards.quote: in one reconstructed patch, cells arborising in the inner margin of the IPL had on average more sustained responses.
cards.section: Inside the W3 circuit: amacrine diversity and layer depth

cards.front: Why can a rare retinal ganglion cell type still have an essential physiological role?
cards.back: Cell abundance does not measure function. A sparse type can carry a signal crucial for a response, so census share alone cannot rank physiological importance.
cards.quote: A type's share of the census says little about its job.
cards.section: Abundance is not importance
